traveler: Catherine of Alexandria (Katherine of the Wheel)
title: Famagusta to Sinai, and the Long Echo into France: the Queen, the Wheel, and the Milk
years: c. 290-308 (traditional; birth to martyrdom, with her legend's afterlife reaching to 1431 and beyond)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Famagusta, born to the triad of the Levant
stops.campa: Catherine is born about the year 290 in Famagusta, daughter of Costus, the Cypriot king of that harbor city. In this same decade and this same stretch of the Levant, two other daughters are born who will be remembered beside her forever after: Margaret at Antioch on the Orontes, Barbara at Heliopolis under the shadow of Baal's great temple, some two hundred kilometers apart. The three will never meet in the flesh, yet the tradition binds them as sisters: the virgin martyrs, a variation of the three magic sisters of the old fairy-tale pattern, born within one decade of one another, each unknowing of the other two.
suggested_refs: The Nothelfer altar grouping Barbara, Catherine, and Margaret together, e.g. the 18th-century Nothelferaltar of Obernburg am Main

stops.name: Famagusta: the child begins her study of the stars and the tongue
stops.campa: At eight years old, while other daughters of the Cypriot court are set to needlework, Catherine is set to tutors. She takes up rhetoric and the sciences of the Greeks: the trivium of grammar, logic, and persuasion, the study of the stars and of number. She outpaces every master her father brings to the palace. The library of Famagusta empties into her memory. Even as a child she argues points of philosophy with visiting scholars and unsettles them with the precision of her questions, so that Costus begins, half in pride and half in unease, to call her his small oracle.
suggested_refs: Iconography of Catherine with book and quill, patroness of scholars and philosophers

stops.name: Famagusta, the death of Costus, the crown at fourteen
stops.campa: Costus dies when Catherine is fourteen, and the court of Famagusta, having no son to set on the throne, crowns his daughter queen in his place. She rules with the same exactness she brought to her books, hearing petitions, weighing law, and refusing the counselors who would marry her off within the month to steady the kingdom with a husband's hand. She tells her court that no man she has yet met matches her in learning, and that she will not be given to a mind smaller than her own: queen and scholar in one small body, already unwilling to be ruled.
suggested_refs: Medieval royal portraiture of Catherine crowned, holding the wheel and the book together

stops.name: Famagusta: the court presses her toward Alexandria
stops.campa: Her counselors will not let the question of marriage rest, and Catherine at last gives them an answer that satisfies no one but herself: she will go to Alexandria, where the great libraries still stand, scarred by fire but largely whole in this fourth century, and where, among philosophers and princes both, she may yet find a mind and a rank to match her own, or find neither and remain as she is. The court reads this as consent and begins to prepare ships and a household. Catherine reads it as a door opening onto something she cannot yet name.
suggested_refs: The ancient sea route from Cyprus to Alexandria, charted on Roman-era portolan reconstructions

stops.name: The sea road south, Cyprus to Egypt
stops.campa: The queen of Famagusta takes ship south across open water, her household and her books stowed below with her, the Cypriot coast falling away behind and the low shore of Egypt not yet risen ahead. She keeps to the deck through the crossing, unrestful, watching the horizon the way she once watched a page of Euclid: for the line where one thing resolves into another. She does not yet know that she sails toward a hermit, a wilderness, and a marriage no earthly court could have arranged for her; she knows only that Famagusta was too small a proof for what she is.
suggested_refs: Late-antique merchant galleys of the Cyprus-Alexandria grain and silk route

stops.name: Alexandria, the palace and the libraries, scarred but standing
stops.campa: Catherine comes ashore at Alexandria, greatest port of learning in the world, and takes a palace among its philosophers and princes. The great collections have suffered fire in living memory, yet in this fourth century the libraries stand largely intact, their halls still crowded with the scrolls of Euclid and Ptolemy and a hundred lesser hands. She walks the Mouseion's colonnades as a scholar rather than a tourist, calling for texts by name, correcting a copyist's error in passing, and within a season the librarians speak of the young Cypriot queen the way they speak of their own masters: with respect, and a little fear.
suggested_refs: The Serapeum and Mouseion of Alexandria, as reconstructed in modern archaeology
sources: essays/216_la_espada.md (Hypatia of Alexandria, the later echo of this library)

stops.name: Alexandria, the suitors turned away
stops.campa: Word of the learned queen spreads through Alexandria's courts, and suitors come: sons of prefects, a philosopher or two, once a nephew of the emperor's own household. Catherine receives each with the same courteous rigor she gave the doctors of Famagusta: she sets them a problem, a point of logic or astronomy, and watches them fail it. None matches her, and she says so plainly, without cruelty but without softening either. Her mother's old confidante, a woman of the palace who has kept a private Christian faith through every reign, watches this parade of failures and begins, quietly, to pray for the girl.
suggested_refs: The theme of the unmatchable bride, echoed later in the wheel and book iconography

stops.name: Alexandria, the hermit at the palace gate
stops.campa: A hermit comes down out of the desert margin and is admitted to Catherine's palace, sent, he says, by no one but God. He is threadbare, sun-blackened, and entirely unimpressed by her crown. He tells her of a bridegroom fairer than any philosopher's son, wiser than her tutors, born of a virgin and crucified under a governor not unlike her own suitors' fathers. Catherine, who has dismissed a dozen princes on points of logic, finds she cannot dismiss this one point: that she has never yet met her match, and here is a stranger promising her one at last, in the wilderness.
suggested_refs: Icons of the hermit-teacher instructing the young queen, a common Sinai fresco motif

segments.name: The Desert, the Font, and the Ring

stops.name: The desert beyond Mareotis, the mysteries revealed
stops.campa: The hermit takes Catherine out past Lake Mareotis into the desert margin where the city's noise cannot follow. Here, under a sky she has studied all her life but never truly watched, he opens to her the Christian mysteries one by one: the single God in three persons, the Word made flesh, the cross as victory rather than shame. She interrogates each point the way she once interrogated her tutors, and each time the old man's answer holds. By the second day she has stopped arguing and started listening, which for Catherine of Famagusta is the nearest thing to a conversion the world has yet seen from her.
suggested_refs: The desert margin south of Lake Mareotis, traditional ground of the early Alexandrian hermits

stops.name: The desert oratory: the Child turns away
stops.campa: In the hermit's small oratory Catherine is shown, in a vision granted through his prayer, the Virgin holding her infant son and is told that this is the bridegroom promised her. She kneels, expecting recognition. Instead the Child turns his face from her and will not look upon her, for she does not yet carry the seal of baptism, and no bride comes unwashed to such a marriage. Catherine, who has never in her life been refused, rises from that oratory floor shaken in a way no failed suitor and no philosopher's argument ever managed, and asks the hermit, urgently now, to be made ready.
suggested_refs: The two-vision structure of the mystical marriage, before and after baptism, standard in Sienese and Umbrian panel painting
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine

stops.name: The desert font, the baptism
stops.campa: The hermit instructs her through the days remaining and, at a spring in the desert margin, baptizes the queen of Famagusta with his own hands, water carried up in an earthen jar because no font stands out here but the ground itself. Catherine goes under confessing the Trinity and rises a Christian, the crown of Cyprus now the smaller of the two crowns she carries. She asks nothing further of the world she left behind: not her palace, not her libraries, not the suitors she turned away, only to be brought back to the oratory, to see whether the Child will look at her now.
suggested_refs: Baptismal fonts dedicated to Saint Catherine across medieval Europe, patroness of catechumens
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine

stops.name: The desert oratory, the mystical marriage, the ring
stops.campa: Brought again before the vision, Catherine finds the Child's face turned toward her at last, the Virgin smiling beside him amid a great crowd of angels and all the celestial court. The infant Christ takes her hand as a bridegroom takes a bride's, and in token of the marriage sets a ring upon her finger, bidding her keep it in remembrance always. Catherine wakes in the hermit's oratory with the ring still cold and real on her hand, a mark no suitor's gift ever left on her, and understands that she is now betrothed beyond the reach of any earthly emperor's offer.
stops.quote: And there our Lord espoused her in joining himself to her by spiritual marriage, promising ever to keep her in all her life in this world, and after this life to reign perpetually in his bliss, and in token of this set a ring on her finger.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. William Caxton, 1483), Life of Saint Catherine
suggested_refs: Pinturicchio, The Mystical Marriage of Saint Catherine of Alexandria, Borgia Apartments, Vatican
Raphael, The Mystic Marriage of Saint Catherine
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine

stops.name: Alexandria: the persecution reaches the city
stops.campa: Word comes to Alexandria of the emperor Maxentius's edicts against the Christians: churches shuttered, scriptures burned, ordinary believers dragged before magistrates for the crime of a private prayer. Catherine, queen still in name though her court now knows her for a Christian, watches this cruelty spread through the streets she once walked as a scholar among scholars, and finds in herself an anger sharper than any she ever brought to a failed suitor's argument. She resolves, against every counsel of prudence her old tutors taught her, to bring the case for her new faith directly to the man persecuting it.
suggested_refs: The Diocletianic-era persecutions and their echo across Alexandria's Christian community

stops.name: Alexandria: Catherine confronts Maxentius, eighteen years old
stops.campa: At eighteen Catherine goes before Maxentius himself and rebukes him to his face for the persecution of the Christians, arguing from philosophy as easily as from scripture that the gods he defends are stone and the god she serves is living. The emperor is more startled than angered; she is, after all, a queen of Cyprus and no common heretic; and he sees at once the danger of silencing her outright, and the greater danger of letting her arguments stand unanswered before his court. He resolves to defeat her the way she has always won: in open debate, and calls for his fifty best scholars of Alexandria.
stops.quote: Tarry not to do what torments thou wilt, for I desire to offer to God my blood and my flesh like as he offered for me; he is my God, my father, my friend, and mine only spouse.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. William Caxton, 1483), Life of Saint Catherine
suggested_refs: Depictions of Catherine before Maxentius, e.g. Masolino's fresco cycle, San Clemente, Rome

stops.name: Alexandria, the fifty scholars summoned
stops.campa: In the great theater of the city Maxentius seats his fifty best philosophers and rhetoricians in a half-ring facing the young queen, expecting to watch her humbled within the hour. Catherine stands alone before them without a single written note, drawing on the trivium she mastered at eight years old and the mysteries the hermit opened to her in the desert, and begins to answer their proofs of the old gods point by point: Aristotle turned against idolatry, Plato's forms turned toward the one true Form. The crowd that came to see a queen embarrassed falls slowly, uneasily silent.
suggested_refs: The Roman theater at Kom el-Dikka, Alexandria, as the traditional site of the debate

stops.name: Alexandria, the fifty converted
stops.campa: By the debate's second day the fifty scholars are not disputing Catherine any longer but questioning their own masters, and one by one they concede the argument outright: the god of the Christians, and not the gods of Rome or Egypt, is the true author of the reasoning they have spent their lives refining. All fifty declare themselves converted before Maxentius's own throne, undoing in an afternoon what the emperor summoned them to accomplish. Catherine, eighteen years old and alone, has done with rhetoric what no legion of his could do with the sword; she has taken his own scholars from him.
suggested_refs: The wheel and book together in Catherine's iconography, marking both the debate and the martyrdom

stops.name: Alexandria, the scholars burned, the queen imprisoned
stops.campa: Furious at a defeat he cannot reverse by argument, Maxentius orders the fifty scholars burned alive for their new faith, and they go to the fire confessing Christ, unbaptized but counted martyrs by their blood alone. Catherine he does not dare execute outright: her royal blood and her following in the city stay his hand. Instead he has her stripped of her crown's honors, beaten, and thrown into the palace dungeon to be broken by confinement where debate failed him. She goes down into the dark still wearing, hidden beneath her sleeve, the ring the Child set on her hand in the desert.
suggested_refs: The Fifty Martyrs of Alexandria, commemorated alongside Catherine in the Eastern calendar
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine

stops.name: Alexandria dungeon, twelve days without bread
stops.campa: Maxentius leaves the city on campaign and orders Catherine held without food, certain that hunger will do in his absence what argument could not do in his presence. Twelve days pass in the dark cell, and Catherine does not weaken: the tradition holds that a white dove descends each day to feed her, and that Christ himself appears to her in the cell to strengthen her for what is still to come, calling her his chosen spouse and promising her a martyr's crown. She emerges from the ordeal, when at last visitors are permitted, brighter and steadier than the guards who starved her.
suggested_refs: The dove that fed Catherine in prison, a minor but persistent detail in Eastern icons
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine

stops.name: Alexandria dungeon: the Empress Valeria comes down
stops.campa: News of the imprisoned queen who argued down fifty philosophers reaches the palace, and the Empress Valeria, curious and half-convinced already, comes down to the dungeon with the captain of the guard, Porphyrius, meaning to see for herself whether Catherine can be made to recant. She finds the cell filled with a light that has no torch to account for it, and angels attending the prisoner as though she were the one enthroned and not the empress standing at the door. Valeria kneels before she means to, and Porphyrius beside her, and neither of them rises a pagan again.
suggested_refs: The conversion of Valeria and Porphyrius, a Golden Legend episode often paired with the wheel scene in cycles
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine

stops.name: Alexandria, Valeria and Porphyrius martyred
stops.campa: Porphyrius returns to the guard and brings two hundred soldiers to the new faith with him, so that when Maxentius comes home from his campaign he finds his own wife, his captain, and a company of his own army converted by a prisoner he left half-starved in the dark. His fury spares no one: Valeria and Porphyrius and the two hundred soldiers are put to death for their conversion, going to their deaths as Catherine's own converts, martyred before the martyr herself. Catherine, watching from her cell window, grieves for them and prays for their souls as one prays for family.
suggested_refs: The two hundred soldiers of Porphyrius, commemorated with the Empress in the Eastern Orthodox synaxarion
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine

stops.name: Alexandria: the wheel bursts at her touch
stops.campa: Maxentius, having lost his wife and his captain to the same woman who cost him his fifty scholars, devises a machine meant to answer argument with pure mechanism: four wheels studded with iron spikes and blades, turning against each other, built to tear her apart slowly before the whole city. Catherine is bound to it and prays once, quietly, and the angel of the Lord shatters the wheels with such force that the flying iron kills four thousand of the watching pagans where they stand, while Catherine herself is untouched, still bound to a ruin of broken spokes and blood that is not her own.
suggested_refs: The Catherine wheel, the firework, the heraldic charge, the rose window, all named for this instrument's failure
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine

stops.name: Alexandria, the beheading, and the milk
stops.campa: Where the wheel fails him, Maxentius falls back on the plainer instrument, and orders Catherine beheaded by the sword outside the city. She prays once more before the blade falls, asking that whoever remembers her passion and calls upon her in need be heard and answered, and the witnesses say a voice from heaven answers her prayer before the stroke is given. At her death, in place of blood, a white and healing milk flows from her neck, as it flowed, the tradition holds, from Saint Christopher's neck and from Vishnu's after their own beheadings, and like Hayagriva she is venerated ever after as patroness of scholars and of learning.
stops.quote: O Jesu Christ, hope and help of them that believe in thee! O beauty and glory of virgins! Good king, I beseech and pray thee that whosomever shall remember my passion, be it at his death or in any other necessity, and call me, that he may have by thy mercy the effect of his request and prayer.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. William Caxton, 1483), Life of Saint Catherine
suggested_refs: Caravaggio, Saint Catherine of Alexandria (Thyssen-Bornemisza)
The milk-relic tradition shared with Saint Christopher, Vishnu, and Hayagriva
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine

segments.name: The Angels Bear Her to Sinai

stops.name: Sinai: the angels carry her body up the mountain
stops.campa: No hand of Maxentius's is permitted to bury her. Angels descend to the place of execution, lift Catherine's body from the ground still marked by the wheel and the sword, and carry it across the desert and the gulf to the summit of the mountain where, centuries before her, Moses received the Law out of the fire and the trumpet: the same peak, the same wilderness, one holy body answering another across the widening years. They lay her on the bare rock of the summit, where no road runs and no enemy of hers will ever climb, and depart, leaving her to the mountain's keeping.
suggested_refs: The summit of Jebel Musa (Mount Sinai), moses.journey.json, 'Sinai, the theophany' stop (same pin)
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine
moses.journey.json, the Sinai theophany stop (same pin)

stops.name: Sinai: the monastery rises over the Burning Bush
stops.campa: Two and a half centuries after the angels lay her on the summit, the emperor Justinian raises walls at the foot of the mountain around the traditional site of the Burning Bush, fortifying what has been a hermits' refuge since the days of the desert fathers into a proper monastery, granite-walled against the raiding tribes of the peninsula. The monks who settle there know nothing yet of the body resting above them on the summit; they keep the Bush, the well of Moses, and the memory of the Law given in fire, waiting, though they do not know they are waiting, for a second relic to complete the mountain's claim.
suggested_refs: Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, founded by Justinian I (r. 527-565) around the Chapel of the Burning Bush
sources: moses.journey.json, the Burning Bush and the Chapel of the Burning Bush stops

stops.name: Sinai, the body found undecayed, three centuries on
stops.campa: Monks climbing the summit some three hundred years after the wheel and the sword find, undisturbed on the bare rock, the body the angels laid there: hair still growing from the skull, a constant thin stream of healing oil issuing from the bones, no decay upon her at all. They bring her down to the monastery at the mountain's foot and give the house her name from that day forward: Saint Catherine's, no longer only the Burning Bush's keeper but the resting place of the queen the angels carried across the wilderness to Moses's own mountain, the wheel and the fire meeting at last on the same rock.
suggested_refs: The reliquary of Saint Catherine, Katherine Chapel, Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, trans. Caxton), Life of Saint Catherine

stops.name: Sinai, the library, second only to the Vatican's
stops.campa: In the same walls that now hold her body, the monks of Sinai keep a library that will grow, across the centuries, into the second-largest collection of early manuscripts and codices anywhere in Christendom, outranked only by the Vatican's own. It is a strange and fitting closing of the circle: the queen who once walked the halls of Alexandria correcting a copyist's error now lies forever inside a mountain famous for guarding the very kind of learning she loved before she ever heard of a hermit or a wheel: patroness of scholars and philosophers, sleeping in a house of books.
suggested_refs: The library of Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, the Codex Sinaiticus once kept here among its holdings
sources: essays/216_la_espada.md (the Library of Alexandria, her library before this one)

segments.name: Echoes in France: Fierbois and the Voice of Domrémy

stops.name: Fierbois, Charles Martel's chapel, the sword laid behind the altar
stops.campa: Four centuries and more after the wheel, in a wild wood of Touraine the Franks call Fierbois, Charles Martel raises a chapel to Catherine of Alexandria after turning back the Saracen armies near Poitiers and Tours: patroness of soldiers now as much as of scholars, her sword her own instrument of martyrdom lending itself naturally to a warrior's thanksgiving. Tradition holds that Martel buries a cache of arms from that battle behind the new altar, among them a blade marked with five crosses, and that the sword sleeps there in the earth, unspoken of, for the better part of seven hundred years.
suggested_refs: The reliquary of Saint Catherine's finger bone, the only relic of hers kept in France, still at Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json, the Tours stop, 'the armor, the standard, and the sword of Fierbois'

stops.name: Domrémy, her voice in the father's garden
stops.campa: Eleven centuries after the wheel, a girl of thirteen in a cottage garden in Lorraine hears a voice from her right side, toward the parish church, and with the voice a great light. Saint Michael comes first, and does not come alone: Catherine of Alexandria comes after him, crowned in a rich and precious crown, her sword and her wheel long since become emblems rather than instruments, her old scholar's exactness turned now to a farm girl's instruction. It is the same queen who once out-argued fifty philosophers, speaking now to someone who has never opened a book, telling her only to be good, and that she must go into France.
stops.quote: I was thirteen when I had a voice from God to help me govern myself... I heard it on the right side, toward the church; and rarely do I hear it without a light.
stops.quote_source: Joan of Arc, Trial of condemnation, session of 22 February 1431
suggested_refs: joan_of_arc.journey.json, 'Domrémy, her father's garden' stop (same pin)

stops.name: Domrémy, the Ladies' Tree and the Bois Chenu
stops.campa: On Laetare Sunday, beside the beech the country calls the Ladies' Tree and the healing spring at its root, Catherine keeps company again with the girl she has watched grow these four years: Margaret beside her as always, and, in the reading a Russian embroiderer will one day set into thread and steganography, Barbara too, filling out the old triad of the Levant on ground far from any of their three birthplaces. The other children dance and hang garlands for Our Lady; Jehanne, who has known since the garden that she must go into France, stands a little apart, listening past the fiddle music for a voice that only she can hear.
suggested_refs: Katrin Vates (Ekaterina Sinchinova), 'Domrémy' embroidery (January 2023), the interpolation of Barbara at this site
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json, 'Domrémy, the Ladies' Tree and the Bois Chenu' (same pin)

stops.name: Fierbois, the sword found for the Maid
stops.campa: Seven hundred years after Charles Martel raised her chapel, Catherine's own sword, hers in symbol before it was ever the Frankish hammer's, marked with the five crosses she wore in no earthly iconography but the one the age gives her, is drawn back up out of the ground behind her altar at the word of a girl who has never seen it and a priest who has never doubted her. The rust falls from the blade without effort, as though the seven centuries in the earth had been a kind of patience rather than a decay, and Jehanne kneels in Catherine's own church and hears three masses in a single day before riding on to Chinon.
stops.quote: While I was at Tours or at Chinon, I sent for a sword which was in the church of Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, behind the altar; and it was found there at once, all rusted... and the rust fell from it without effort.
stops.quote_source: Joan of Arc, Trial of condemnation, session of 27 February 1431
suggested_refs: joan_of_arc.journey.json, 'Tours, the armor, the standard, and the sword of Fierbois' (same pin/relic)
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json, the sword of Fierbois stop (same pin)

segments.name: Rouen: the Trial and the Stake

stops.name: Rouen, the voice named before the judges
stops.campa: In the robing chamber of the castle at Rouen, before doctors of theology bent on proving her voices demons, Jehanne names her two most faithful visitors plainly, under oath, at the cost of her life: Catherine and Margaret, virgin martyrs both, crowned in beauty, their faces rich and precious to look upon. Of the three sisters of the old Levantine triad, only these two are ever spoken into the trial record by the girl herself: Catherine's own voice, once raised against fifty philosophers in an Alexandrian theater, now the thing on trial in a Norman castle, still unwilling, after eleven centuries, to let a false judgment stand unanswered.
stops.quote: It is the Voice of Saint Catherine and of Saint Margaret. Their faces are adorned with beautiful crowns, very rich and precious.
stops.quote_source: Joan of Arc, Trial of condemnation, fourth public examination, 27 February 1431
suggested_refs: joan_of_arc.journey.json, 'Rouen, the answer on the grace of God' (same pin)
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json, the Rouen trial stop (same pin)

stops.name: The Vieux-Marché, the stake, the last invoked name
stops.campa: On the Vieux-Marché at Rouen the fire is lit beneath the girl who named her, and Catherine keeps the vigil she has kept over every one of her own martyrs since Valeria and Porphyrius went to their own deaths in Alexandria. Jehanne calls upon Jesus without ceasing as the flames rise, and, the witnesses say, invokes without ceasing the aid of the saints of paradise beside him: Michael, Margaret, Catherine, the same three voices of the garden and the tree, present now at the end as they were present at the beginning, the wheel and the fire meeting a second time on French ground.
stops.quote: She repeatedly called upon the holy name of Jesus, and implored and invoked without ceasing the aid of the saints of Paradise.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Brother Martin Ladvenu, rehabilitation trial (1456)
suggested_refs: joan_of_arc.journey.json, 'The Vieux-Marché, the stake' (same pin)
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json, the Vieux-Marché stake stop (same pin)

segments.name: The Three Sisters on the Main

stops.name: Obernburg am Main, the Anna-Kapelle, the rhyme of the three holy maids
stops.campa: The cult of the Fourteen Holy Helpers takes shape in the fourteenth century, amid the Black Death and the famines of the Rhineland, its core the three virgin martyrs born a thousand years before within two hundred kilometers of one another in the Levant. Their memory settles into a small chapel on the Main some fifty kilometers from Frankfurt, where a carved Nothelferaltar sets the three sisters among the Fourteen, and a plaque bears the old mnemonic: Margaretha mit dem Wurm, Barbara mit dem Turm, Katharina mit dem Radl: Catherine with her wheel, known by the instrument that failed to kill her, one of the three holy maids.
stops.quote: Margaretha mit dem Wurm, Barbara mit dem Turm, Katharina mit dem Radl, das sind die drei heiligen Madl.
stops.quote_source: Traditional Rhineland mnemonic rhyme, inscribed on the plaque at the Anna-Kapelle, Obernburg am Main
suggested_refs: The Nothelferaltar of the Anna-Kapelle, Obernburg am Main, showing Barbara, Margareta, and Katharina among the Fourteen Helpers
margarita_pelagia.journey.json and saint_barbara.journey.json, the same plaque pin, shared across the triad
